items.title: The Building Wouldn't Cool Down
items.excerpt: The first heat wave of summer brought messages from tenants about weak cooling. I changed a clogged filter, checked the rooftop equipment, and kept working after the easy fix was gone.
items.reason: Published post is under 700 words; add concrete but non-invented depth for AdSense/content quality.
addedParagraphs: The hardest part of a heat call is that comfort and safety start to blend together. A cool hallway does not help much when a tenant is stuck in a hot bedroom. A small improvement at the equipment does not feel like progress to the person sitting beside a fan, waiting for the air to change.

That is why I try to separate what I know from what I only suspect. I can say the filter was changed. I can say the rooftop units were checked. I can say the airflow was still weak in some places. What I cannot do is promise the whole building will cool down by a certain hour when the system has not given me that answer yet.
items.currentContent:
The texts started early that morning. A few tenants said the air coming from their vents felt weak. Others said it was moving, but it was not cold enough to make any difference. At first I thought it might be the usual start-of-summer trouble. By the time I reached the building, it was already over 30 degrees outside, my phone kept buzzing, and it was clear the problem was bigger than I had expected.

My maintenance guy was checking units while I went up to the roof. The condenser units were running, just not the way they should have been. I changed a clogged filter. That helped a little, but not enough. I went back downstairs knowing I had fixed one problem without fixing the building.

## A filter was not going to solve the day

More messages came in around noon. Everyone wanted to know when the cooling would be back to normal, and I did not have a good answer. One resident said the unit felt like an oven and messaged me again while I was on the roof. I felt bad, but I still could not give a repair time. People were hot in their own homes. They did not want a lesson about mechanical systems. They wanted an answer.

I explained that we were checking it and that this was not a switch I could flip. I am not sure anyone felt better after hearing that, but making up a repair time would have been worse.

Our custodian brought water to some of the tenants in the hottest units. My maintenance guy checked vents and made sure nothing obvious was blocking the airflow. I checked thermostats and went back over what I had already looked at. The equipment seemed to be running, yet the building was still not cooling properly.

## The portable-air-conditioner question

One tenant stopped me in the hallway and asked whether we could bring in portable air conditioners. I understood why he asked. When your unit feels like an oven, a portable machine sounds like the quickest answer.

The problem was scale. We were not dealing with one bedroom. We had complaints from enough units that a handful of portable machines would barely make a dent. They might help in a specific urgent situation, but they were not a repair for the building system.

I gave our property manager an update around two. At that point I could tell her what we had checked, what had improved, and what had not. I still could not tell her exactly what was wrong.

That bothered me. I like closing the loop. I like finding the bad part, fixing it, and telling people the problem is handled. This was not that kind of day.

## Knowing when the answer is not in front of you

I went back to the roof and tried bleeding air from the lines because my maintenance guy thought it might be part of the problem. I was not convinced, but it was one more reasonable check. The sun was beating down, the units were still struggling, and the messages kept coming.

By late afternoon I was thinking we might need a cooling specialist. I knew what we had checked, but I still did not know why the building was not cooling properly.

It is the same reason I ask residents to give useful details when they report a problem. “The AC is broken” gets my attention, but the room, time, airflow, and temperature help me act. I wrote about that in [No, I Can't Read Your Mind: Why Reporting Building Issues Matters](/blog/no-i-cant-read-your-mind-why-reporting-building-issues-matters).

As the day wound down, my phone was still full of messages and the cooling system was still not right. My maintenance guy and I would have to keep working through it and keep residents updated.

items.title: The Scooter in the Middle of the Hallway
items.excerpt: At 7:30, I moved someone's e-scooter out of the hallway. The tire marks were annoying, but the real problem was a rider passing too close to a resident who walks with a cane.
items.reason: Published post is under 700 words; add concrete but non-invented depth for AdSense/content quality.
addedParagraphs: The other piece is consistency. If one scooter is allowed to sit outside a door, the next person will ask why theirs cannot. If staff only respond after a complaint, residents learn that the rule depends on who notices first. That is not fair to the person using the cane, and it is not fair to the staff trying to keep the building safe.

I also have to keep the conversation practical. Most people are not trying to create a hazard. They are trying to get in, plug in, and move on with their day. But convenience cannot take over the path everyone else needs to use. A hallway is shared space before it is anyone’s shortcut.
items.currentContent:
At seven-thirty in the morning, I was moving somebody's e-scooter out of the middle of the hallway. It was not leaning against a wall or tucked into a corner. It was parked dead centre, like nobody else used the floor.

In a building with older tenants, children, and people using mobility devices, that is more than an annoyance. It is a trip hazard sitting in the route everyone depends on.

My maintenance guy watched me move it and shook his head. He had been scrubbing black tire marks off the walls and floors for weeks. The rubber leaves long streaks that need the right cleaner and a lot more work than the rider probably imagines.

He told me people would keep doing it until something happened. I did not like hearing that, mostly because he might be right.

## The conversation by the elevator

Around noon, a tenant stopped me near the elevator. I am leaving out her name and floor. She walks with a cane and said a young rider had almost clipped her the week before.

She did not fall. That does not make it harmless.

I told her we were working on it. She gave me the look people give when they have heard that sentence before. We had sent letters. I had knocked on doors. I had repeated the same conversation with several households. The hallway would improve for a week and then another scooter would show up.

From her side, another notice probably looked like more paper without a result. I could not blame her for being skeptical.

The scooter problem reminds me of [why underground parking cannot become a storage room](/blog/why-your-underground-parking-garage-is-not-a-storage-unit). Different part of the property, same issue. One person's convenient storage can create a hazard for everyone else.

## Telling people no is not a storage plan

I kept coming back to the same question: if scooters cannot sit in the hallway, where should residents put them?

A secure storage area near the entrance might help. Clear signs near the elevators and stairwell doors might help too. If the safer option is also the easier option, most people will probably use it.

I was also thinking about clearer signs near the elevators and stairwell doors, along with updated lease language that spells out what happens after repeated violations. “Please be considerate” had not been enough.

## The cleaning work is real work

The tire marks may look minor beside the safety issue, but they still matter. My maintenance guy is the person on his knees with a scrub brush while the rider is upstairs and probably has no idea how much work one trip down the hall created.

Dirty, marked hallways also change how the building feels. Residents who take care of the place notice when common areas start looking neglected. Staff notice too. It gets harder to ask people to respect a space when the damage is allowed to pile up.

That is why cleanup cannot be the whole response. We can remove the marks today and have them back tomorrow if the riding continues.

## What I can do next

I do not have a perfect solution yet. I can keep the walking route clear, speak privately to the responsible households, and stop sending vague warnings that disappear into the same pile as every other notice.

I can also keep pushing for a practical storage option. Once residents have a reasonable place to leave a scooter, the individual conversations become simpler. The hallway is not storage, and there is another place to use.

If that does not change the behaviour, the next step will be formal notices. Moving one scooter while ignoring another would make the rule look optional.

I expect I will have to move another scooter before this is solved. For now, the main concern is simple: the tenant who walks with a cane should be able to reach the elevator without watching for somebody riding around the corner.
